item.title: New material gets stronger the more it bends
item.description:
In Brief WashU chemists have created a polymer that gets stronger the more it’s bent and strained. The material mimics biological materials in the human body, including collagen, which gives skin its strength and elasticity. The material could have medical applications, particularly in protecting and repairing tissues.

Most materials get weaker with use. But a team led by Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, has created a polymer that defies the usual laws of wear and tear.

“Our smart material actually gets stronger the more it’s bent and strained,” Ke said. “It has properties we have never seen before. It can remember, adapt, learn and grow. We’re excited to think about the possible applications.”

The breakthrough was described in a study published online in Nature Materials. Co-authors include graduate students Yufei Chen and Mingliang Bai and postdoctoral researcher Dan Zheng .

The patented polymer, created in Ke’s lab with compatibility for 3D printing, is made from a biodegradable blend of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound often used in laxatives and other health products. The mixture forms a hydrogel, a flexible material that can absorb and retain large amounts of water.

In tests, Ke and his team applied the material to a flexible, knee-like joint. “We bent it 10,000 times, and the material performed just as we predicted,” Ke said. “The polymers in the hydrogel become more uniform and organized, making it stronger in exactly the places where the strain is happening.”

The smart material owes its strength and adaptability to cyclodextrin, a sugar-based compound that forms ring-shaped structures. When the polymer is stretched or bent, these rings slide into position to reinforce the areas under strain. “These moving rings are critical to the structural design,” Ke said.

In many ways, the material mimics biological materials in the human body, including collagen, a protein that gives skin its strength and elasticity. “Some of the most impressive smart materials are found in biology,” Ke said. “We used nature for inspiration.”

Spreading word to researchers, investors

Ke believes the polymer could have medical applications, particularly in protecting and repairing tissues.

“Because it’s made of sugar and polyethylene glycol, it’s completely compatible with biological tissues,” Ke said. “We expect this material to attract interest from surgeons or orthopedic medical device companies who are looking for new approaches.”

For example, the material could be used to support artificial joints or to repair damaged tissues. In either case, areas that aren’t subjected to stress or strain would remain soft and pliable. “If you’re putting material into a body, you don’t necessarily want it to be completely rigid,” Ke said. “The material gets stronger only where it’s needed.”

Ke is a chemist, not an orthopedist or medical device specialist, and he acknowledges that other experts may recognize applications he has yet to consider.

“We want to work with experts at WashU Medicine and elsewhere to explore the possibilities,” Ke said. “Hopefully this paper will help us get the word out to researchers and potential investors.”

So far, Ke and his team have produced the material in small quantities, just tens of grams at a time. But with the concept successfully demonstrated, they believe production could scale up to meet demand.

The new polymer builds on Ke’s broader research into creating innovative materials inspired by nature. In April 2025, he proposed a new generation of smart fabrics at A&S Innovates, Arts & Sciences’ inaugural research pitch competition.

“We’ve shown it’s possible to produce smart materials with a 3D printer and the right chemistry,” Ke said. “We see a lot of possibilities.”

D Zheng, Z Yu, Y Chen, CD Smith, M Bai, EHR Tsai, J Liu, W Zhang, S Lin, C Ke. Mechanical adaptation drives out-of-equilibrium network reorganization and self-strengthening in adapt-ring networks. Nat Mater. 2026 Nov 5.

DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02795-0

Following the widespread community adoption of the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 series, we are pleased to introduce Qwen3.8, the most capable generation in the Qwen open-model family to date.

Built on the architectural foundation of Qwen3.5, Qwen3.8 delivers substantial gains across coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks. Qwen3.8-27B brings these advances to a compact, deployment-friendly dense model: a native vision-language model that understands images and videos, with flexible thinking control, designed to carry complex, multi-step tasks through to completion with greater reliability.

Qwen3.8 Highlights

Qwen3.8-27B features the following enhancements:

Core Capabilities: Comprehensive improvements across coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks.Agent Execution: Stronger autonomous planning and better handling of environment feedback, leading to more reliable end-to-end task completion.Downstream Compatibility: Broader support for popular harnesses and development tools, making it easier to integrate into your existing stack.Flexible Thinking Control: Thinking mode is on by default and can be disabled per request; reasoning depth can be tuned with reasoning_effort, and reasoning context from historical messages is retained via preserve_thinking.Vision-Language Understanding: Native support for image and video understanding, from STEM diagrams and documents to hour-scale videos.Model OverviewType: Causal Language Model with Vision EncoderTraining Stage: Pre-training & Post-trainingLanguage ModelNumber of Parameters: 27BHidden Dimension: 5120Token Embedding: 248,320 (Padded)Number of Layers: 64Hidden Layout: 16 × (3 × (Gated DeltaNet → FFN) → 1 × (Gated Attention → FFN))Gated DeltaNet:Number of Linear Attention Heads: 48 for V and 16 for QKHead Dimension: 128Gated Attention:Number of Attention Heads: 24 for Q and 4 for KVHead Dimension: 256Rotary Position Embedding Dimension: 64Feed Forward Network:Intermediate Dimension: 17,408LM Output: 248,320 (Padded)MTP (Multi-Token Prediction): trained with multiple stepsContext Length: 262,144 natively and extensible up to 1,000,000 tokens.Best Practices

To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following settings:

Sampling Parameters: We suggest using the following sets of sampling parameters:

Thinking Mode: temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=0.0, repetition_penalty=1.0Instruct (or non-thinking) mode: temperature=0.7, top_p=0.80, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0

For supported frameworks, you can adjust the presence_penalty parameter between 0 and 2 to reduce endless repetition. However, using a higher value may occasionally result in language mixing and a slight decrease in model performance.

Adequate Output Length: To optimize performance on agentic tasks, we recommend allocating sufficient output length to allow the model to generate detailed and comprehensive responses. For frameworks that support separate token limits for internal reasoning and final outputs, we suggest the following configuration within the 1M context length:

Reasoning Content: Set the maximum output length to 262,144 tokens.Final Response: Set the maximum output length to 131,072 tokens.

These settings provide the necessary capacity for complex reasoning while ensuring ample space for high-quality final deliverables.

Processing Ultra-Long Texts: Qwen3.8-27B natively supports context lengths of up to 262,144 tokens. For long-horizon tasks where the total length (including both input and output) exceeds this limit, we recommend using RoPE scaling techniques to handle long texts effectively, e.g., YaRN.

Long Video Understanding: To optimize inference efficiency for plain text and images, the size parameter in the released video_preprocessor_config.json is conservatively configured. It is recommended to set the longest_edge parameter in the video_preprocessor_config file to 469,762,048 (corresponding to 224k video tokens) to enable higher frame-rate sampling for hour-scale videos and thereby achieve superior performance. For example,

{"longest_edge": 469762048, "shortest_edge": 4096}

Alternatively, override the default values via engine startup parameters. For implementation details, refer to: vLLM / SGLang.

item.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
item.description:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.

The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."

Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.

Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."

Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.

Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.

Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.

Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."

Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.

Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.

Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."

"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

item.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
item.description:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

item.title: Latent Introspection: LLMs Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
item.description:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

[Submitted on 23 Feb 2026 (v1), last revised 7 Nov 2026 (this version, v3)]

Title:Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept InjectionsView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.9%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety. item.title: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
item.description:
Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange.

Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know.

Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.

Exchange on premises in 2026Section titled “Exchange on premises in 2026”

Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out.

Microsoft has not announced the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online:

Exchange 2016 and 2019 are out of support. Both reached end of support on 14 October 2025. Microsoft sold a paid Extended Security Update programme for a while, and according to press reports of an Exchange team statement, it ended in October 2026 with no further extension. Servers still running those versions receive no fixes of any kind.No new features. Exchange Server Subscription Edition (SE) is now the only supported on-premises Exchange, and there will be no more major versions after it. SE does not receive the features developed for the cloud. Even its first cumulative update has slipped from late 2025 to an undetermined date in 2026.The new Outlook does not support it. Microsoft’s own documentation for the new Outlook for Windows says it plainly: “On-premises Exchange accounts aren’t supported.”The APIs are moving to the cloud. New functionality ships only on Microsoft Graph, a cloud API. Exchange Web Services in Exchange Online started being switched off in October 2026 and will be gone entirely in April 2027.

None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud.

For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year.

Outlook without ExchangeSection titled “Outlook without Exchange”

The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client.

Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies.

With Stalwart 1.2.0 the users do not need to change anything. The administrator moves the mailboxes and points the DNS records at Stalwart, and users connect with the same Outlook they used before.

Supported protocols and clientsSection titled “Supported protocols and clients”

Stalwart implements the following Microsoft protocols, all served on the same HTTPS port as JMAP and the WebUI:

MAPI over HTTP (EMSMDB and NSPI), the native protocol of classic Outlook for Windows, in both cached and online mode. It covers mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes, incremental synchronisation, the global address list and the offline address book, delegate access, shared mailboxes, rules, junk email settings, reminders, search folders and read receipts.Exchange Web Services, schema versions Exchange 2010 SP2 to Exchange 2016: mail, calendars, contacts, tasks, folders, sharing and delegates, free/busy, inbox rules, out of office, name resolution, distribution lists, and streaming and pull notifications.Exchange ActiveSync 14.1 and 16.1: mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes, with push through Ping, meeting responses, search and out of office.Autodiscover in its POX, SOAP and JSON dialects, so clients configure themselves from an email address and a password.

That set of protocols is what the following clients use to talk to an Exchange server, and they can connect to Stalwart the same way:

Classic Outlook for Windows (Outlook 2016 and later, including Microsoft 365 Apps), over MAPI over HTTP and EWS.Outlook for Mac, over EWS.Apple Mail, Calendar and Contacts on macOS, through an Exchange account over EWS.Mail, Calendar and Contacts on iPhone and iPad, through an Exchange account over ActiveSync.Android mail apps with Exchange account support, such as Gmail, Samsung Email and Nine, over ActiveSync.Thunderbird, with its built-in Exchange support for mail over EWS, or with TbSync for calendars, contacts and tasks over ActiveSync.Evolution (through evolution-ews) and eM Client, over EWS.Libraries and tools built on EWS or ActiveSync, such as exchangelib.Shared dataSection titled “Shared data”

The Exchange protocols are not a separate silo inside Stalwart. They are another door into the same accounts. A message filed in Outlook is in the same mailbox an IMAP or JMAP client sees, a meeting accepted on a phone appears in the calendar that CalDAV clients read, and a contact added in Apple Contacts shows up in the CardDAV address book. A user can keep Outlook on the office desktop, the native mail app on a phone and a JMAP webmail in the browser, all on one account.

Rules created in Outlook’s Rules and Alerts are stored on the server as mail rules, which run as Sieve when the message is delivered. They apply when Outlook is closed and whatever client the user opens next. Delegates and folder permissions set in Outlook become regular Stalwart shares, so they apply to every protocol. Shared mailboxes open automatically in Outlook from group membership, as they do with Exchange.

Not every part of an Exchange deployment has a counterpart. Stalwart does not offer public folders, archive mailboxes, mobile device management, RPC over HTTP (Outlook 2010 and earlier) or NTLM and Kerberos sign-in: clients authenticate with a password, an app password or OAuth. The Exchange documentation covers configuration, DNS and Autodiscover, each family of clients, and the differences from Exchange that administrators should know about before a migration.

New OutlookSection titled “New Outlook”

One Outlook is missing from the list above: the new Outlook for Windows, the one that Windows now installs by default and that classic Outlook keeps offering through a toggle in its title bar.

The new Outlook does not work with Stalwart, and it does not work with any self-hosted server, Exchange included. It is built to work through Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft does not support on-premises Exchange accounts in it at all.

The new Outlook does accept IMAP accounts, and that might look like a way around the problem. It is not. When an IMAP account is added to the new Outlook, the connection to the mail server is not made from the user’s computer. As heise and c’t reported in November 2023, the new Outlook sends the IMAP server name, the user name and the password to Microsoft, and Microsoft’s cloud connects to the mail server on the user’s behalf. Every message then passes through Microsoft’s infrastructure on its way to the screen. Microsoft does not only see the mail; it holds the password to the mailbox.

For an organisation that runs its own mail server to keep its data under its own control, this defeats the purpose of the whole exercise. We advise against using the new Outlook with any self-hosted email deployment, whether it runs Stalwart or anything else. Users who see the “Try the new Outlook” toggle in classic Outlook should leave it off.

The same applies on phones. Outlook for iOS and Android reach on-premises mailboxes through a Microsoft cloud service as well, which requires a hybrid Exchange Online setup. On mobile devices, the native mail, calendar and contacts apps, which connect directly over ActiveSync, are the better choice.

Late to the partySection titled “Late to the party”

The obvious question is why Stalwart is adding Exchange protocols now. EWS is being removed from Exchange Online, Microsoft’s own future for Outlook is a cloud client, and classic Outlook is reportedly supported until 2029. Why build support for protocols that will be obsolete in a few years?

Because the companies that run Exchange today cannot wait a few years, and because those protocols are the bridge they need to cross.

An organisation with a few hundred Outlook users cannot replace its mail server and its mail client in the same weekend. It can replace the server, though, if nobody notices. With Stalwart speaking the Exchange protocols, the server moves first: mailboxes are migrated, DNS records change, and on Monday every user opens the same Outlook and the same phone apps they used on Friday. The organisation’s mail is back under its own control from day one, and no one’s work is interrupted to get there.

The client can then change at the pace that suits the users. Over time, as classic Outlook reaches the end of its life and the new Outlook remains tied to Microsoft’s cloud, we expect users to move gradually to third-party email clients built on open standards, and in particular on JMAP. Outlook will stop being an option for anyone who cares about where their email lives, and by then the people who used it will have had the time to choose something else without a deadline over their heads.

Exchange support is not where Stalwart is going. It is how organisations get from where they are to where Stalwart is.

Footprint and modularitySection titled “Footprint and modularity”

Exchange compatibility is not a small piece of work. It adds about 200,000 lines of code to Stalwart, and we know that some of you would rather not carry that weight if you never plan to see an Outlook client. We built it with that in mind, so that it costs as little as possible for those who do not use it, and so that it can be removed cleanly once the Exchange protocols are obsolete:

It is a separate module. All of the Exchange code lives in its own crates, behind a single exchange Cargo feature. Build Stalwart without that feature and every line of Exchange code is left out of the binary. The compilation guide shows how. The day the Exchange protocols have no users left, removing them from the codebase is largely a matter of deleting those crates and that feature.It is disabled by default. Even in the official builds, which include the module, the Exchange protocols are off until an administrator enables them. While they are disabled, the server behaves as if they did not exist.It stores nothing until it is used. Outlook and the other Exchange clients keep properties that no standard protocol has a place for: extended properties, reminder state, client settings. Stalwart stores them as metadata attached to the item they belong to, using the JMAP Object Metadata extension, and only writes them when an Exchange client connects and sets them. Accounts that are never opened by an Exchange client carry no Exchange data at all.Its data can be removed. Because the Exchange-specific properties live in that metadata and not in the messages, events and contacts themselves, deleting the metadata removes every trace of them while the items stay intact for IMAP, JMAP, CalDAV and CardDAV clients.Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365Section titled “Migration from Exchange and Microsoft 365”

A drop-in replacement is only useful if the data can follow. Vandelay, our account import and export tool, migrates mailboxes from both sides of Microsoft’s offering:

Exchange Server on premises, through the EWS importer, which reads mail, calendars and contacts.Microsoft 365 (Exchange Online), through the Microsoft Graph importer, which reads mail, calendars, contacts and OneDrive files. The EWS importer also works against Exchange Online, for as long as Microsoft keeps its EWS endpoint running.

Vandelay copies each account into Stalwart over JMAP, and the domain moves to Stalwart when its MX records and client settings change. The migration guide for hosted services walks through the whole process, from the first test account to the cutover. With the Exchange protocols enabled on Stalwart, Outlook and the other Exchange clients then connect through Autodiscover and find the migrated mail, calendars and contacts.

Other changes in 1.2.0Section titled “Other changes in 1.2.0”

Exchange support is the headline, but 1.2.0 brings several other features, most of them developed alongside it because an Exchange replacement needs them:

Mail rules. Server-side rules in the familiar “when a message matches these conditions, do this” form, managed in the WebUI, over JMAP or from Outlook. Conditions cover senders and recipients, subject and body, headers, size, attachments, importance, message type, mailing lists, spam score, date ranges and weekly schedules. Actions include moving and copying, marking as read or as junk, forwarding, replying with a template and rejecting. Rules are compiled into Sieve together with the vacation response. Each account also gets junk email lists: blocked senders, safe senders and safe recipients. See Mail rules.Read receipts. Message Disposition Notifications (RFC 8098), including the JMAP methods for sending and parsing them (RFC 9007).Working hours. Per-account working hours, managed in the WebUI, over JMAP or through CalDAV. Time outside working hours appears as unavailable in free/busy lookups, and a new setting lets users of the same organisation see each other’s free/busy time without sharing calendars explicitly. See Availability.Rooms and equipment. Resource accounts with a capacity, a location and delegates who manage the calendar, with invitations booked automatically or approved by hand. See Resources.Native FoundationDB client. A new asynchronous Rust client replaces Apple’s libfdb_c library. It needs no client library on the host and is now part of the standard build and Docker image. In our benchmarks it delivers between 4.5 and 6.9 times the throughput of the previous client on point reads, with 5 to 7 times lower median latency and about half the CPU.

The changelog lists every change and fix, along with the upgrade steps: existing servers need to add the new permissions to their default roles.

Stalwart CLI 2.0Section titled “Stalwart CLI 2.0”

Last week we also released version 2.0.0 of stalwart-cli, and its biggest addition is an interactive console. Run stalwart-cli with no arguments in a terminal and it opens a full-screen interface that covers the same ground as the WebUI: browsing and editing accounts, domains and every other configuration object, watching the dashboard, following live traces and running actions. It is aimed at administrators who live in SSH sessions, or who work on hosts where opening a browser is impractical.

The console is built with Ratatui, the excellent Rust library for terminal user interfaces, and it is schema-driven like the rest of the CLI: its screens, forms and field help come from the schema that the server publishes, so it picks up new objects without being updated. The CLI also learned to sign in with the OAuth device flow and to remember the session, so a single approval in the browser is enough for both the console and every subsequent command.

FOSDEM 2027Section titled “FOSDEM 2027”

Stalwart will be at FOSDEM 2027 in Brussels. We will have a Stalwart stand, and on Saturday, 30 January 2027, we will give a talk about moving from Microsoft Exchange to Stalwart in the Modern Email devroom. If you are planning a migration away from Exchange, or are curious about what it takes, come and talk to us. We will post the time and title of the talk once the schedule is published.

Until then, the Exchange documentation has everything needed to try it, and we would love to hear how your Outlook clients get on with Stalwart.

item.title: Freeing the iPod Nano 5G
item.description:
A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through ipod_sun, a font-based exploit. Whether the same approach would work on the 5G was still an open question.

I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit. My motivation was simple: an up-to-date music player without an internet connection. I built a fully untethered boot chain that loads Rockbox from the nano 5Gâs NAND, with no computer or button sequence needed after installation. I also found a way to make the existing exploit fully untethered on the nano 7G, and likely the 6G too.

Existing DFU exploits, including q3kâs wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time. I used wInd3x to explore the device and develop a convenient, fully untethered exploit. The firmware details below refer to the latest nano 5G firmware, 1.0.2 (34A20020).

The catch with ipod_sun

The nano 5Gâs NAND flash appears through a flash translation layer (FTL) as a logical disk with 4 KiB sectors. Its partition table separates a small private area for persistent device state, a firmware partition containing boot programs and resources, and a data volume for user files. The firmware partition has a directory of named images; the fonts live inside rsrc, a resource volume formatted as FAT16.

The original ipod_sun chain combines a resource-validation bypass with a font-parser vulnerability. Appleâs firmware directory identifies the normal operating system as osos, the disk-mode program as disk, and the resource image containing fonts as rsrc. The disk-mode boot path does not request the resource signature check used by normal OS boot.

Swapping the disk and osos directory entries exploits that difference: selecting disk mode now launches Appleâs regular OS under the disk-mode policy. The OS still reads its fonts, but the bootloader has not required a valid signature for the modified resource image.

The font then triggers CVE-2010-1797, the FreeType CFF stack-overflow vulnerability also known through the star exploit. A malformed font program corrupts the parserâs stack and redirects execution. My 5G port adapts that technique to the deviceâs font and execution context.

The swapped images remain on disk, but each restart still requires choosing disk mode with the deviceâs buttons. A normal boot selects the other entry. I wanted a better experience, with the modified font loading through the normal OS path.

Finding a bypass in the normal boot path

The bootloader is organized into EFI-style modules stored as Portable Executable (PE) images. The module that passes execution to the next boot stage decides whether to validate rsrc. It first asks the PrivateData module for FirmwareStatus, which comes from an authenticated record in the private NAND partition.

The decisive branch is below. This is reconstructed C from the reverse-engineered routine, with unrelated fuse handling and protocol setup omitted.

A value of 2 returns success before the resource-validation query. Bit 0 must remain clear: it is checked first, so 3 would reject the boot attempt. Tracing the restore OS shows that it sets the status to 1 during firmware transfer and clears it to 0 at the end. This suggests an update-in-progress guard that prevents booting an incomplete installation.

Appleâs resource-mount path writes status 2 only on the first successful boot, after rsrc has passed signature verification. My hypothesis is that this avoids repeating signature verification to shorten boot time or reduce energy use.

This is the second bypass. Instead of disguising the normal OS as disk mode, I can leave the firmware directory alone and supply a valid private record with bit 1 set. The normal boot path then accepts the modified resource image, and its font delivers code execution automatically.

The record lives in the private partition, identified by MBR type 0x3e. On the 5G layout I examined, the partition begins at logical block 1, with 4 KiB blocks. The bootloader reads a 512-byte header from its start. The status-bearing format begins with the little-endian magic PRVD and has this layout:

The fields needed to understand the bypass Offset Value or purpose 0x00 0x44565250 (PRVD) 0x04â0x0c Three 32-bit words: 2, 0, 4 0x40 32-bit FirmwareStatus; use 2 0x80 16-byte device-bound integrity tag

The integrity tag is device-specific, so creating and saving a valid PRVD record requires code execution on that iPod.

The tag is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-1 digest, encrypted with the deviceâs hardware AES UID key, selected through key slot 2. It authenticates the private header, but as the authentication is constructed on device we can falsify it if we have code execution.

Using emCORE to make it persistent

To inspect and update the private partition, I adapted emCORE, an older framework from freemyipodâs earlier iPod exploitation and boot work. It provided an existing USB-controlled environment to extend for the 5G.

I wrote the nano 5G NAND driver and integrated it into emCORE alongside the flash translation layer (FTL) and hardware AES access. Iâll cover the flash memory sequencer subsystem (FMSS), which enables NAND writes, in a future post. The FTL presents logical sectors over physical flash; it is the layer through which I read and write the private record and install the modified font.

The private-status tool verifies the existing header and tag, constructs the updated record, and obtains its new tag from the device. It rechecks the partition table and header before writing, then flushes the write and reads it back. The tool writes a complete 4 KiB logical sector even though the bootloader only consumes the smaller header. This works on nano 5G hardware.

Once the private record and modified font are installed, they remain in NAND across restarts. emCORE and the host computer are needed for the installation workflow, not for each subsequent boot.

A bootloader in less than 28 KB

Reaching the font parser automatically solved persistence. The next constraint was fitting something useful inside the font. I wanted it to load Rockbox from storage, so the payload needed a NAND driver, a flash translation layer, a filesystem reader, and enough startup code to hand off reliably.

From the font slot to the main payload ceiling Component Calculation Font slot 165,416 font bytes Font container Subtract 78,312 font bytes Fixed overhead, excluding the stub Subtract 1,056 font bytes, leaving 86,048 Ã3 encoding Each code byte uses three font bytes: â86,048 Ã· 3â = 28,682 code bytes Cleanup stub Subtract 808 code bytes for cleanup and handoff to the bootloader Main payload ceiling 28,682 â 808 = 27,874 bytes

To fit, I compiled with size and link-time optimizations and had the linker remove unused sections. The Rockbox kernel is stored on the deviceâs FAT32 partition and can be easily updated.

Taking control from the font parser

Code execution initially arrives in a damaged FreeType call frame. The stack has been corrupted, and Appleâs OS has left interrupts, DMA controllers, timers, caches, and address translation configured for its own use. Jumping straight into a large C program would carry that state into storage initialization.

I split the bootstrap into two images. The first is the 808-byte assembly stub at 0x22050000. Its job is to leave the parser context: mask IRQs and FIQs, switch to a private stack, stop inherited timer activity, quiesce DMA and clock domains, and clean up caches and the MMU before entering the main payload. It replaces the damaged stack and then jumps to the Rockbox kernel loader.

The second image is the main loader at 0x22060000. Its entry code disables the watchdog before starting the NAND scan, installs its own stack, and clears the uninitialized-data area before calling C. The watchdog matters because reconstructing the logical flash mapping can take several seconds; a reset in the middle would stop the boot before it ever found Rockbox.

This separation keeps the most fragile stage small. The assembly stub establishes a controlled execution environment; the main payload can then do the more substantial storage work in freestanding C.

Reading NAND and starting Rockbox

At the hardware level, the NAND driver uses FMSS, a programmable microcontroller, to communicate with the NAND chips. lemonjesusâs earlier work on the S5L8702 sequencer, published as S5L8702-FMISS-Tools, documents its instruction set and provides tools for inspecting and building bytecode. That research is important prior work for understanding this part of the storage hardware; my work here uses the sequencer to read NAND as part of the nano 5G boot path.

The loader first checks that the microsecond timer used for driver timeouts is running. It then initializes the read-only NAND and FTL stack, mounts the FAT filesystem, and opens /.rockbox/rockbox.ipod. The core sequence follows the Rockbox bootloaderâs own file-loading path:

The file loader checks the Rockbox model identifier and checksum, then leaves the executable image at 0x08000000. The final handoff keeps interrupts masked, cleans and invalidates caches, drains pending writes, and branches to that address. Rockboxâs startup code takes over from there. If storage, mounting, or image loading fails, the payload shows the failing stage on the LCD and stops.

Result and limits

On my nano 5G, the result is a cold, battery-powered boot straight into Rockbox, with no USB connection and no disk-mode button sequence. The PRVD partition setting skips rsrc validation and, when combined with the star exploit, enables untethered boot straight into Rockbox. The main constraint is that the font payload is limited to 27,874 bytes. Installation and restoration procedures, along with the reverse-engineering notes and build details, are in the nano5g_bootstub and nano5g_emCORE repositories below.

I have confirmed that the private-data partition works the same way on the nano 7G, which suggests the method will likely work on the 6G too. I plan to get the nano 4G and 5G Rockbox ports into good shape before applying this method to the 6G and 7G.

References nano5g_bootstub: the font exploit, PRVD analysis, two-stage Rockbox loader, and exact size budget. nano5g_emCORE: the emCORE port, NAND read/write tools, authenticated private-record updates, and installation procedure. CUB3Dâs ipod_sun: the earlier nano 6G/7G chain combining the disk-mode swap with a modified font. q3k, âwInd3x, the iPod Bootrom exploit 10 years too lateâ: the USB/DFU entry point used to run unsigned code during setup, with background on the iPod boot chain. Appleâs firmware update catalog: lists nano 5G firmware 1.0.2 (34A20020) under iPod software family 34. CVE-2010-1797: the existing FreeType CFF vulnerability used by the font exploit. freemyipodâs emCORE source: the original framework and earlier device targets on which the nano 5G adaptation builds. lemonjesusâs S5L8702-FMISS-Tools: earlier reverse engineering of the flash-controller sequencer, with instruction-set documentation and bytecode tools. n3g_fmss: my documentation of the nano 3G flash memory sequencer. n4g_fmss: my documentation of the nano 4G flash memory sequencer. Rockbox source: upstream firmware, storage, filesystem, and image-loading code reused in this work.

item.title: The search for a top dark matter candidate
item.description:
The Search for a Top Dark Matter Candidate Was Losing Hope. Then Came a Potential Signal. Will It Be Enough to Energize the Struggling Field? Physicists were growing weary with WIMPs, one proposed contender for the particles that make up dark matter. Despite their new cautious optimism, many challenges remain

Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career. The lab’s panoramic views of white-capped mountains and endless greenery are nearly inescapable. Physicists fuel their work with sharp espressos, rather than the watery coffee many Americans accept.

The lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers. Nestled beneath 4,600 feet of rock is an array of particle detectors. Thanks to the mountain’s thick skin, these instruments are shielded from cosmic rays, the high-energy particles produced by black holes, exploding stars and even our own sun. In the quiet depths of this laboratory, physicists hope to pick up on much more elusive particles—including dark matter.

For the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up 85 percent of the matter in our universe. One primary target has been weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs—a hypothesized candidate for dark matter that passes through normal matter with barely a trace. Massive underground detectors like those at Gran Sasso are leading the search.

But no one has definitively found a WIMP, so no one is sure that they exist—and challenges to spotting them are building. As detectors get more sensitive, new background signals are beginning to cloud them, reducing the odds of catching WIMPs. Funding is growing more precarious, leaving many wondering how many years this endeavor has left.

When I visited the lab in May, the mood among some of these physicists was muted. “Of course, we were a bit more depressed,” reflects physicist Paolo Salomone, laughing. Despite his clear enthusiasm for the dark matter hunt, Salomone, a strikingly blue-eyed University of Chicago postdoctoral scholar, knew he was entering a field some might diagnose as terminal.

Then, in September, a pinprick of hope emerged. An American lab also searching for WIMPs released a preprint paper detailing a single—but intriguing—data point, rising above the expected background signals. Maybe, just maybe, it was dark matter.

Salomone was on vacation in Corsica when his phone started blowing up. Text notifications from physicist friends streamed in, asking him if he’d seen the news. “I was there on the beach trying to look at my phone, trying to zoom in on the plot,” he says. Watching the faraway excitement, he says, “I felt like I was missing out a lot.”

The finding was not a definite dark matter detection—one data point isn’t nearly enough to count as a discovery. Still, the result spawned headlines across the globe, a torrent of preprint papers and newfound hope for many physicists in search of WIMPs.

The question, now, is what’s next. Will this life raft be enough to overcome the field’s growing challenges? And will the few other detectors with similar sensitivity—most notably, one at Gran Sasso—be able to replicate the signal?

Nearly a century ago, Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed a group of galaxies with some moving so quickly that they should have escaped the cluster’s gravity and flown apart. He theorized that some invisible material was gluing them together. Since then, scientists have accrued more evidence for this dark matter: stars speeding precipitously fast around a galaxy’s rim; unexpectedly strong gravitational lensing, in which distant light is bent by extreme gravity.

To explain it all, astrophysicists dreamed up WIMPs in the 1980s. As far as subatomic particles go, these would be relatively massive. In theory, they glide through space, on occasion lightly interacting with matter. Physicists have a pretty good sense of the density of dark matter scattered throughout our universe, but not much more about it. “It opens the possibility of having a lot of light particles or very few heavy particles,” says Salomone.

Directly detecting WIMPs, then, could clue us into the mass of individual dark matter particles and the number of them floating around, as well as how strongly these particles interact with normal matter. But finding them has been a challenge. Not only are physicists searching through a vast plain of possibilities, but they’re also looking for incredibly rare interactions that require extreme care in detection.

The smallest impurities can anger a detector. To illustrate the point, Marcello Messina, the technical coordinator for Gran Sasso’s XENONnT experiment, brought up the humble banana. While we don’t tend to think of a banana as radioactive, the fruits are rich in potassium, leading to a tiny shower of particle decays. “A banana can completely destroy our data table,” he said.

Messina was my guide for the day at Gran Sasso, driving me six miles through one of Italy’s longest tunnels and into the mossy interior of the mountain. He led me through the lab’s sterile halls, ending up at his even more sterile detector.

Messina’s XENONnT experiment is a hulking cylinder that holds a chamber of nearly 9.5 tons of xenon—mostly liquid—inside. The hope is that when a WIMP flies into the detector, it jostles one of the large and stable xenon atoms, which would in turn shoot out electrons and a light ray, alerting sensors to the strange particle’s presence.

XENONnT, which has been collecting data for around six years, is the strapping great-grandchild of the team’s original 2006 prototype. “XENON, for almost all its life, provided the most sensitive results,” Messina told me. “It was definitely leading the field.” Today, a few more rivals—like the American detector—have emerged.

We walked past another device that looked like a gigantic red Lego: a new detector Salomone is helping to build, DarkSide-20k, which will use a chamber of around 55 tons of argon instead of xenon. This enormous detector will reach a similar sensitivity to XENONnT and is set to begin collecting data in 2028.

Despite their materials’ purity, physicists expect some level of background fuzz—mainly radioactive decay products—and predict what that will look like. Sometimes, though, this “background” can behave in unexpected ways, so physicists must have a high bar for what anomalies in their data to take seriously.

Messina showed me a kind of memento mori for physicists: the latest generation of the DAMA experiment, which made a claim of dark matter detection that has been dismissed by most of the community.

In 1997, DAMA, which is made up of sodium iodide crystals, detected a signal that varied yearly, swooping in every summer—just as dark matter was expected to do. But while the team has continued to stand by their results, other experiments later ruled this out.

After DAMA’s false alarm, “I think people are just very cautious now,” says Ina Sarcevic, a physicist at the University of Arizona.

Despite the fear of more detector-cried-wolf scenarios, many physicists quickly pulled together theories to explain September’s announcement of a possible detection, Sarcevic says. The signal came out of South Dakota’s LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, which is currently the world’s largest WIMP detector.

Physicist Richard Gaitskell, LZ’s spokesperson, has been searching for dark matter for nearly 40 years, starting with a detector “barely bigger than the top of my thumb,” he says. LZ, on the other hand, is a nine-foot-tall cylinder containing around 11 tons of xenon, packed within a 20-foot-tall outer structure.

To take advantage of LZ’s whopping size and sensitivity, Gaitskell says, the team “decided to really aggressively push” beyond the usual search parameters.

The longstanding assumption in these experiments has been that WIMPs swoop in at relatively low energies and bounce off the xenon like billiard balls. In this case, when a WIMP collides with a xenon nucleus, it scatters the atom’s protons and neutrons in what’s called a “coherent” manner, where their resulting energies add up, amplifying the signal. But if WIMPs were to barrel in at higher energies, the particles would scatter in a trickier way to track.

It was the switch to searching for these higher-energy collisions that led to LZ’s unusual detection. The signal also hinted that particles of dark matter would be quite heavy and collide with matter in a different way than many expected. Rather than rebounding like billiard balls, the WIMP may lose some energy (and mass) in the crash, exiting as a different, slimmer form of dark matter.

Notably, this detection couldn’t be explained by known forms of background events, like stray neutrons. The signal, then, could be dark matter, but it may also be a previously unknown type of background.

In announcing this event, Gaitskell says, the team was looking for input from the wider community, as they continue to pore through their own data. And input he did receive.

Amid the excitement and wave of preprint papers, though, many have retained a sense of caution. Messina says he was initially skeptical of the single data point. “The immediate reaction was, ‘Come on, one event?’” he says. But he recognized XENONnT’s potentially crucial role in the next step toward discovery.

Given their detector’s comparable sensitivity, the team is now rushing to replicate the finding, looking through the past two years of their own data for signals that chime with the American detection. Or they could find nothing.

Either way, Messina would like to let the team’s data analysis do the talking, rather than get too excited now. They hope to release a paper in the next few months. “Data matters,” Messina says. “All the rest is fake.”

When Messina led me around in the spring, he wasn’t optimistic about the future of his field. He was continuing to support the search for dark matter with XENONnT, but he had also been devoting time to detecting neutrinos, another kind of subatomic particle generated by stars, radioactive decay and the Big Bang. “Many people like me are thinking, ‘You know what, I want to investigate different fields,’” he said.

Some WIMP proponents point out that even though the detectors haven’t found one of these fabled particles, they have made a less obvious kind of progress over the decades. In their searches, scientists have ruled out many potential WIMP masses and densities, ticking away at the options and possibly making it easier to zero in on their true properties in the future.

But to many onlookers—including the funding bodies that control cash flow—the lack of clear progress in particle physics has been disappointing. “It’s quite hard to convince politicians to support you if you have a significant discovery each 30 years,” Messina said.

On top of the current fragile science funding ecosystem in the United States, he wasn’t sure how much more time WIMP detection had. He doubted the proposed next-generation detector, XLZD—which would dwarf LZ and XENON and merge the collaborations—would move forward.

After LZ’s finding, though, Messina’s tune has changed. While he still stresses the uncertainty that this signal will lead to a discovery, he believes it has imparted “some momentum” back into WIMPs.

Many physicists still see more promise in other dark matter models—the hypothetical WIMPs might not be the best (or only) explanation.

Ben Safdi, a theoretical physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, says that LZ’s detection may well be dark matter, but his initial excitement has waned. At first, the signal seemed to match an existing theory for WIMP behavior, but several preprint papers—including one of his—challenged this idea. “My personal belief that it is dark matter has gone down,” he says.

Safdi divides his research between WIMPs and a different dark matter candidate called axions. These theorized particles would move in a “continuous, almost fluid” wave through the universe, he says. Individually, axions would be super light—much less massive than WIMPs—but together, they could account for the missing mass of dark matter.

Attention to axions has surged as people have grown tired of WIMPs. While Safdi still thinks the WIMP hunt is worth continuing, “my heart is in axions,” he says.

Did you know? Other strategies to find WIMPs

Some scientists hope to indirectly detect WIMPs by looking for neutrinos produced when they collide with their proposed antimatter counterpart and annihilate. Others are hoping to create WIMPs. According to some theories, WIMPs might be produced by energetic collisions between normal particles.

Even if interest in WIMP detection is revitalized, technological challenges remain. One specter still haunting the field is a fog of neutrinos that’s threatening to descend on the instruments.

With increased sensitivity, the detectors are starting to pick up the constant swarm of neutrinos. These tiny particles don’t interact much with matter—trillions move through your body every second—but they can clutter data taken by detectors that are precise enough to notice them. As this neutrino fog wafts in, potential WIMP signals could get lost in the haze. XENONnT reported its first glimpses of the fog in 2024.

This isn’t a huge problem for the detectors yet, and not everyone agrees it will be soon. But once neutrinos start meaningfully gumming up the signal, scientists don’t know what they’ll do.

Ronald Walsworth’s group is experimenting with a workaround: tracing the direction of incoming particles. WIMPs are expected to flood in like a “headwind” against the solar system’s path through the galaxy, he says. On the other hand, a lot of neutrinos emanate from the direction of the sun, produced by the churn of fusion.

A sea of liquid xenon functions “like an antenna,” says Daniel Ang, a quantum scientist in Walsworth’s group. The flash of light only clues scientists into a particle’s collision—not the direction it rode in. So to trace a signal’s source, physicists might have to take a whole new approach.

Walsworth decided to try this by using a more glamorous substance: diamonds. From his previous work, he knew that when particles cut through diamond crystals, they leave behind a finely detailed track—so their incoming direction is clear. “That’s the grandiose idea we had,” says Walsworth, a quantum physicist at the University of Maryland.

But the team has only tested their blinged-out detector on a small scale, and getting the funds to go bigger will be a challenge—especially given the “sagging of enthusiasm” for WIMPs, Walsworth says.

Once Salomone, the postdoc, got back from vacation, his excitement about LZ’s signal was slightly tempered by his boss, he says. “He was, of course, more skeptical and less enthusiastic than me.”

But even among Salomone’s liquid argon detector community, scientists are paying serious attention to the result. His collaboration has a regular meeting, which only one or two dozen people usually show up to. But at a recent one, some 100 people attended. Even people who never participated were interjecting with ideas, he says.

Salomone’s workdays are much like before, continuing to help build the DarkSide-20k detector, placing orders for special screws and popping over to the café for an espresso. But he feels a renewed excitement about the theory behind his daily tasks.

“You’re still doing what you were doing before but with a different mind-set,” he says. “Spending more time trying to read papers, spending more time trying to be even a better physicist, so that’s what I’m really happy about.”

item.title: The Power of GraphQL, Without GraphQL
item.description:
COBALT — GraphQL from TypeScript, without writing GraphQL

The Power of GraphQL, without ``GraphQL``. The last framework that actually makes sense, in the age of AI.

Why Cobalt?It's simple and powerful.

It extends GraphQL but doesn't force you to use it manually.

You get the iteration speed of tRPC and the flexibility of GraphQL. This way you're not sacrificing your ability to craft complex & optimized GraphQL schemas for initial speed.

You can refine your API at every stage, without collecting dangerous tech debt.

Why not REST? Endpoint Fatigue & Over-fetching

Managing hundreds of endpoints creates a maintenance nightmare. You fetch huge JSON blobs just to display a username.

The Cobalt Solution

One smart endpoint. The client specifies exactly what data it needs. The GraphQL feature everyone loves.

Why not pure GraphQL? The Double Declaration Problem

You write a TypeScript interface. Then you write a GraphQL Schema. Then you write a Resolver. If they drift, your app crashes.

The Cobalt Solution

Single source of truth. Your TypeScript code IS your schema. No client-side codegen steps or schema sync required.

Why not tRPC? Tight Coupling Trap

Great for monoliths, but your backend logic leaks into your client bundle. Scaling to microservices or exposing a public API later becomes a rewrite.

The Cobalt Solution

Loose coupling, magnetic types. The schema is the contract. You can move fast AND scale to complex backends.

The Cobalt Way Magnetic Type Safety

Define your logic once. The Schema is inferred. The SDK is generated. The types are magnetically bonded across the network boundary.

The Cobalt Solution

The best of all worlds. The speed of tRPC, the flexibility of GraphQL, and the simplicity of REST.

Hate Typing?Thirsty LLM?Less is more.A codebase that is fun to work with. No Boilerplate Stop writing glue code

Traditional frameworks require Controllers, manual serialization, and Service layers just to move data.

The Cobalt Solution

Write your logic. Cobalt generates the transport layer. No routers, no adapters, no manual schemas.

LLM Friendly Context Rot

LLMs struggle with large, scattered codebases. Providing context across 50 files degrades performance and increases cost.

The Cobalt Solution

Dense, collocated code. Smaller context window footprint means smarter AI assistance and lower token costs.

Zero-Config SDK Typed SDKs for free

Writing GraphQL queries manually is tedious and error-prone. Cobalt gives you a fully typed SDK out of the box.

The Cobalt Solution

sdk.query.user({ id })() - Autocomplete your entire backend, as if it was local code. No graphql tags, no codegen watchers.

item.title: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees on Cars
item.description:
S.9348A/A.10411A Prohibits Car Companies from Charging for Built-In Features

Amid Rising Consumer Fees, New Law Increases Price Transparency and Puts Money Back in New Yorkers’ Pockets

Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.

“New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.”

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car. Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down.”

State Senator James Skoufis said, “People ought to know they’re able to use their already-installed remote start or heated seats during the winter without a monthly subscription. This new law will simply and clearly prohibit car manufacturers from ripping off New Yorkers who already paid for vehicle features when they purchased their car. It’s a common sense law and I’m grateful for the Governor and Assemblymember Magnarelli for their partnership enacting this legislation."

Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli said, "I thank Governor Hochul for recognizing the importance of this legislation, particularly as technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace. This law will help protect New Yorkers from unfair fees and ensure consumers aren’t paying extra for features already built into their vehicles.”

The law will take effect in 90 days on February 27, 2027.

This new law is the latest in Governor Hochul’s ongoing commitment to help address the cost of living by putting money back in the pockets of New Yorkers statewide. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, she has:

Secured reforms to lower auto insurance premiums for New Yorkers, battling fraud, limiting damages paid out to bad actors, and ensuring consumers, not insurance companies, are prioritized. Signed legislation requiring businesses to notify consumers of upcoming renewals and price changes as well as provide clear instructions on how to cancel subscriptions. Cut middle-class taxes to their lowest rates in 70 years. Tripled the Child Tax Credit, providing families up to $1,000 per child under the age of four and up to $500 for school-aged children, beginning in 2026. Made school meals free for every student, saving families $1,600 per child every year. Sent Inflation Refund checks to 8.2 million New Yorkers — up to $200 for individuals and up to $400 for families. Increased the maximum weekly unemployment benefit by $300 a week.

item.title: Rune: Rust VM for Emacs
item.description:
R ust UN der E macs video introduction

This project is an experimental Emacs core written in Rust. The project is still at a very early phase but has the following goals:

Bring multi-threaded elisp to Emacs Be “bug-compatible” with existing Emacs Lisp packages (everything should still work) Enable performance improvements (including faster GC, regex, and JSON) by leveraging the Rust Ecosystem.

See the design doc for more details.

The current goal of this project is to create an editor MVP. We have a basic elisp runtime, and we are working on adding basic editing functionality in a minimal GUI. This will include:

buffer text insertion/deletion cursor line wrapping scrolling file IO display tables

If you want to contribute or have ideas for things to add, please open an issue.

Lisp files are currently pulled from

https://github.com/emacs-mirror/emacs/tree/emacs-29.1/lisp

Any modification for bootstrapping contain the tag RUNE-BOOTSTRAP.

cargo run --release -- --repl Load the bootstrapped elisp and open the REPL cargo run --release -- --no-bootstrap --repl Open the REPL with only the builtin functions loaded cargo run --release Load the bootstrapped elisp and exit

Run the test suite with MIRI

MIRIFLAGS='-Zmiri-strict-provenance' cargo +nightly miri test

The project is defined by a main package rune, which depends on the crates included in the crates directory. One of those is the rune-macros crate, which defines the defun proc macro for defining builtin functions. The rest of the code is contained in src/. The modules are described below.

objects The basic objects used in the interpreter. These are modeled after Emacs objects using tagged pointers with inline fixnums. Conversion between different primitives and object types is also found here. reader The Emacs lisp reader that translates a string to a cons cell. Due to the simple nature of lisp syntax, the reader is hand rolled and does not rely on any parsing libraries. env The global obarray. Currently, function bindings are global and immutable and value bindings are thread-local and mutable. When the ability is added to share data between threads, this will enable new threads to safely run functions without the need to copy them. gc Contains the allocator and garbage collector. All code for rooting and managing objects lives here as well. bytecode The bytecode VM. This uses the same opcodes as Emacs and uses the bytecomp.el to compile. interpreter The basic elisp interpreter. This is used only to bootstrap the elisp byte-compiler. fns, data, alloc These modules contain definitions of builtin in functions. Some of these are just stubbed out until the functionality is actually needed.

See the architecture doc for more info on the structure of Rust Emacs internals.

This project is moved forward by trying to load new elisp files and seeing what breaks. The best way to do that is with cargo run, which will load the currently bootstrapped files. The bootstrapped files are located in main.rs as part of the load function.

Usually what is needed is to implement more primitive functions. This is done with the defun macro. For example, if we wanted to implement the substring function, we would first look at the lisp signature.

(substring STRING &optional FROM TO)

Then we would translate the types to their Rust equivalent. If the correct type is not known we can use Object. In this example we would write our Rust signature as follows:

#[defun] fn substring(string: &str, from: Option<i64>, to: Option<i64>) -> String {...}

To load a new elisp file, run cargo run --release -- --load <file>. Files that are not bootstrapped are not yet included in this repo, but are part of Emacs. Once the file is bootstrapped it can be added to the lisp directory.

Rune includes the `assert_elprop!` macro, which enables property testing against GNU Emacs. This macro works by sending the same Lisp form to both Rune and Emacs and then comparing their results. It can also be used in conjunction with the `proptest` crate.

#[test] fn test_addition() { // Verify that (+ 40 2) evaluates to 42 for both Rune and Emacs assert_elprop!["(+ 40 2)"]; } // Verify that make-vector works for any arbitrary byte proptest! { #[test] fn test_make_vector_consistency(size in arb_byte()) { assert_elprop!["(make-vector {} ?A)", size]; } } Define WINEPREFIX: export WINEPREFIX=$PWD/.wine Add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu to rust toolchain: rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu Setup the wineprefix: `./scripts/setup-wineprefix`. This script will install Emacs inside the prefix as well

Now you can run the tests on Windows like that: cargo test --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu. In case you use Nix enviroment you should skip 1 and 2 points.

Also, you can tell eglot to check the code marked with #[cfg(windows)]. Just add the following to .dir-locals.el and restart eglot:

((nil . ((eglot-workspace-configuration . (:rust-analyzer (:cargo (:target "x86_64-pc-windows-gnu"))))))) tagged pointers in Rust My initial approach to creating tagged pointers in Rust. It serves as in intro to this project. implementing a safe garbage collector An overview of the garbage collector used in this project and how Rust enables safe GC abstractions. A vision of a multi-threaded Emacs :: Some ideas about how to add multi-threading to the existing language. Design of Emacs in Rust Some of the unique benefits that Rust could bring to Emacs. Remacs The original Rust and Emacs project. Remacs took the approach of enabling interop between Emacs C core and Rust, enabling them to replace parts of Emacs piecemeal. The project is currently unmaintained but is a big inspiration for Rune. emacs-ng The spiritual successor to remacs. This project integrates the Deno runtime into emacs, allowing you to write extensions in elisp or javascript. Which sounds cool if you happen to be a web developer. It really shows the power of integrating Emacs with a more modern ecosystem (which is part of the promise of Rust). helix A fast modern text editor written in Rust. crafting interpreters This was a big inspiration for this project, and it’s probably one of the best introductions to programming language implementations.

item.title: Making a dumb TV just smart enough
item.description:
Making a dumb TV just smart enough

I own an old, cheap TV. It has no Internet connection, no fancy smart features that make you want to install a Pi-hole, and no ask-me-again-later updates.

However, it is connected to my own desktop computer through an HDMI cable, so I can watch movies and TV series from the couch. Setting it up used to involve going to my desk, enabling the secondary monitor, opening the relevant application, moving its window to the secondary monitor, setting it in fullscreen, going back to the couch, remembering I forgot my wireless keyboard, getting off the couch, grabbing my wireless keyboard, going back to the couch again, and then pressing the Space bar.

The most important quality of a programmer is laziness.

So, of course, I vowed never to get off the couch unnecessarily. And that meant controlling everything from the TV remote.

So, I got myself an IR transmitter and an IR receiver to tinker with:

Then, I fished out an ESP32-C3 Mini devboard, a mini-breadboard, and a handful of jumper wires, and made the most basic device that could solve my woes:

I have played around with Espressif MCUs before, including for early versions of the OmniMorse, but I must admit that Claude is just faster at it than I am. With the help of Opus 5.5, I identified the RC-5 IR codes for each remote button, and set up a few scripts so that a single button press on the remote would do the whole dance I described above.

Problem solved!

But this first success unlocked much more.

I also own a bunch of old consoles. Getting everything hooked up is a chore, and makes a mess of wires. It would be much simpler to run an emulator on my computer and show it on the TV.

Thus, I installed DuckStation, PCSX2, Dolphin, Cemu and ES-DE, configured two Xbox controllers on each of them, and got Claude to start everything from a single button on the remote.

At this point, I was using two of the four colored buttons of the TV remote. So, of course, I had to come up with two more modes. I got Claude to add a Fireplace mode, which just plays 10-hour videos, the most important one being a fireplace. And also Steam, in Big Picture mode.

Soon, there were regular issues with windows opening on the wrong screen, so I switched approaches. Instead of a large desktop on two screens, I resorted to multiseat, which I had always wanted to use, with two separate X sessions, one on each screen. This also allows using both screens at the same time without interference.

But that did mean I could not directly control the windows on the TV from my regular session. So, again, I got Claude to make me an admin panel:

The virtual TV remote actually works, by sending directly through the device I cobbled together. The device also tracks volume being changed from the real remote, so things stay in sync. The rest is just commands to my computer, including a virtual gamepad, and a real-time stream of what is being displayed (mouse clicks work too!). Also, turning on an Xbox controller switches to the emulator or Steam mode, and turning the last one off goes back to the fireplace.

Last, but not least, I took a significant amount of time making (telling Claude to make) everything fast. The whole thing took me about 10 hours in total, most of which was setting up console emulators.

Claude still needs to be kept on a tight leash: it sometimes wanted to go in the wrong direction, left obvious bugs, or suggested fixes that did not address the root cause. However, it saved me a bunch of time on the original problem, and lowered the effort enough to go above and beyond!
